title: Scaling Up Thermodynamic AI Models
abstract: Thermodynamic computing devices based on the Ising model show great promise for low-power AI inference and edge computing, but scalable methods for training large models for such hardware remain limited. Prior theory shows that the time-averaged behavior of high-temperature Gibbs-sampled Ising systems can implement feed-forward neural inference. We turn this theoretical correspondence into a scalable and purely backpropagation-based algorithm for training deep convolutional networks for thermodynamic inference on Ising machine hardware. Our image classification models achieve accuracies of 94.9% on CIFAR-10 and 76.0% on CIFAR-100 under binary Gibbs sampling. We then develop and experimentally validate a mathematical theory relating inference cost to accuracy and controlling autocorrelation times. Subsequently, we calculate asymptotic results showing that inference cost is bounded by a well-controlled tradeoff with performance and exhibit algorithms for computing optimal inference schedules. Finally, we discuss implications for hardware development and the future of high-temperature thermodynamic AI models.
summary: The paper presents a novel framework to train deep neural networks for inference on Ising machine hardware by treating the network as a sequence of thermodynamic blocks. It introduces 'Gibbs regularization' within a backpropagation scheme, allowing high accuracy while keeping computational cost manageable through careful control of sampling parameters.
main_problem: Developing scalable methods for training large Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to run inference on low-power thermodynamic computing hardware based on the Ising model.
main_result: The authors developed a purely backpropagation-based algorithm using Gibbs regularization that successfully trains deep convolutional networks, achieving high accuracy while demonstrating that inference cost is bounded by a controllable tradeoff with performance.
method: Training involves a multi-phase process combining standard loss functions (CE) with specialized fixed-point and magnitude regularizers to stabilize the network weights for operation within stochastic Ising dynamics. Inference relies on time-averaging output spins via Gibbs sampling.
model_or_system: The system is based on deep convolutional networks implemented as sequential 'thermodynamic blocks' operating on an Ising model Hamiltonian. The core computation uses high-temperature Gibbs sampling rather than ground-state annealing.
key_observables: Accuracy (e.g., 94.9% on CIFAR-10), Inference Cost, Integrated Autocorrelation Time ($	au_{	ext{int}}$), and the percentage of FLOPs offloaded to Ising hardware.
important_parameters: Temperature gradient parameter ($\delta$), total number of sweeps ($G$), and various loss weighting parameters ($\alpha, \lambda_{	ext{FP}}, \lambda_{	ext{mag}}$).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the time-averaged behavior of high-temperature Gibbs-sampled Ising systems can accurately emulate feed-forward neural inference. The theoretical analysis relies on linearizing dynamics around mean-field approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall classifier structure (Encoder $	o$ Blocks $	o$ Decoder) and detail the internal architecture of a single thermodynamic block as an Ising system with input, hidden, and output spins.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical correspondence between neural networks and Ising systems to developing the scalable backpropagation training algorithm via Gibbs regularization. It then analyzes error sources (related to $G$ and $\delta$) and concludes by discussing hardware implications for convolutional topologies.
why_interesting: This work bridges statistical mechanics (Ising models, Gibbs sampling) directly into practical AI engineering, providing a concrete roadmap for realizing energy-efficient neuromorphic computing using principles from non-equilibrium statistical physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Our CIFAR-10 classifier. The encoder is a single classical convolution with sign activation. This is followed by six thermodynamic blocks. The classical decoder is a global average pool followed by a fully- connected linear map to the output layer. Each thermodynamic block contains three convolutional layers, as depicted in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Architecture of a single thermodynamic block, implemented as an Ising system. It contains three layers of spins: input spins s0, hidden spins s1, and output spins s2. The input layer s0 is pinned in place. They are connected by bidirectional linear couplings, depicted in purple boxes. Couplings in an Ising system are bidirectional, but the labels indicate the forward coupling, i.e. moving downward in the diagram. The reverse couplings are the linear adjoint; for the exact relationship, see Equation (5). The hidden layer is also affected by the local magnetic fields b. Finally, an average-and-sign circuit a accumulates time-averages of s2 and outputs their signs.
Figure 3: Empirical |z| distribution and 3-component Gaussian mixture fit for the first block of our CIFAR- 10 model.

Figure 4: Measured stochastic error rate compared against numerically evaluated integral for the first block of our CIFAR-10 model. The fit is very close, but the integral does not capture the period-two oscillation caused by the chromatic Gibbs sampling.
Figure 5: Theoretical convergence rate for a single Gaussian spike away from z = 0, with time of transition to power-law convergence visualized.
